analysis.one_liner: Bolsters Medicaid pay for rural hospital maternity care and mandates year-long postpartum coverage.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee markup or a vote; introduced in late September 2024, it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The Keeping Obstetrics Local Act would have required Medicaid to pay rural, critical-access, Indian Health Service, and safety-net hospitals at least 150% of Medicare rates for maternity care, with the federal government picking up the full cost of the increase. It would have sent an annual payment to small hospitals that deliver fewer than 300 babies a year to keep their labor and delivery units open, in exchange for a signed contract to keep providing those services. It also would have made 12-month postpartum Medicaid and CHIP coverage mandatory in every state, let pregnant women get temporary Medicaid on the spot at hospitals and clinics, and required hospitals to give 180 days' public notice before closing an obstetric unit.
analysis.who_benefits: Pregnant and postpartum women on Medicaid or CHIP, especially in rural and underserved areas where maternity wards have closed, along with the small hospitals that serve them. Communities that would have gotten advance warning before a local obstetric unit shut down also gain.

how_it_helps.text: Requires Medicaid to pay eligible hospitals — rural, critical-access, Indian Health Service, tribal, and hospitals where at least half of births are publicly insured or uninsured — at least 150% of the Medicare rate for maternity, labor, and delivery services starting in fiscal 2026, with the federal government covering the full increase.

Creates an annual "anchor payment" for hospitals delivering fewer than 300 babies a year: a revenue floor of $10,000 per delivery plus $1.2 million for standby staffing and equipment, in exchange for a contract to keep labor and delivery services open for at least two more years, with the state allowed to claw back the money if the hospital closes or breaches.

Converts the optional 12-month postpartum Medicaid and CHIP coverage period into a requirement for all states, and requires all states to provide presumptive eligibility so a pregnant woman can be enrolled on the spot without a full eligibility determination first.

Adds a state option for maternity "health homes" offering coordinated pregnancy and postpartum care with a 90% federal match, directs federal guidance on covering doulas and certified midwives, boosts the federal match for perinatal depression and anxiety screening, and lets the U.S. Public Health Service Commissioned Corps be deployed to areas that lost obstetric care.
Requires hospitals to notify the public, state, and local agencies at least 180 days before closing an obstetric unit, and directs collection of data on labor and delivery services and closures.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who would fund 100% of the increase above each state's existing maternity payment rate plus enhanced matching for other provisions, and state Medicaid budgets, which would fund the base increase and absorb new mandates such as mandatory 12-month postpartum coverage and presumptive eligibility.

drawbacks.text: The spending is large and effectively uncapped: the bill sets a 150%-of-Medicare payment floor with a 100% federal match, hard-codes $10,000 per delivery and $1.2 million in standby capacity payments per low-volume hospital for fiscal 2027 before the required cost studies are complete, and authorizes $150 million a year for the Commissioned Corps plus $50 million in state planning grants.

It imposes new mandates on states: every state, including those that declined the option, would have to provide 12-month postpartum Medicaid and CHIP coverage and presumptive eligibility for pregnant women, shifting costs onto states that had chosen not to.

Payments flow to hospitals as institutions, and the design relies on contracts and clawbacks to keep the money tied to actual service; a hospital that closes could leave the state trying to recover funds from a bankruptcy estate, where the bill only gives the state preferred-creditor status rather than a guarantee.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: substantially higher Medicaid spending to keep delivery wards open in places where they are otherwise disappearing, with the money conditioned on hospitals actually keeping services running. The design is more disciplined than a straight bailout — the contract requirement and clawbacks aim payments at keeping care available — but the fixed dollar amounts were set before the cost studies the bill itself would fund, so some hospitals would likely be paid more than their true costs, and states that had opted against postpartum coverage expansions would bear new obligations.

outcome.mechanism: Wyden introduced it in late September 2024 and the Senate Finance Committee never took it up; it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Ron Wyden introduced the Keeping Obstetrics Local Act on September 25, 2024, joined by 17 other Democratic senators as original cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the day it was introduced, and no further action was ever recorded on it.
The bill accumulated 19 cosponsors in total — 18 Democrats and 1 independent — and no Republican cosponsor.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without the Finance Committee holding a markup or the Senate voting on the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Rural hospitals that might have been contractually bound to keep money-losing delivery units open, Medicaid managed care plans that would have faced higher required hospital payment rates, and federal and state taxpayers in the short term all keep the status quo — while communities that continue to lose local obstetric care do not gain anything from the outcome.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals and payers kept the status quo

for.name: Ron Wyden
for.role: U.S. Senator from Oregon; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Keeping Obstetrics Local Act and recruited 17 Senate colleagues as original cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and took no further action — no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 cosponsors were Democrats or independents and no Republican ever signed on, but no Republican ever voted on or formally opposed the bill either — it died in committee without anyone having to take a position on the record.

industries.note: The bill would lock Medicaid in as a guaranteed, above-cost revenue channel for these hospitals — a 150%-of-Medicare payment floor with 100% federal matching plus annual anchor payments — while requiring them, by contract, to keep labor and delivery units open and clawing back money if they do not. For rural mothers, keeping these hospitals in the maternity business is the point of the bill, so the hospitals' financial interest and the public's access interest run together here.

industries.industry: Doulas, certified midwives, and the maternal health workforce
industries.note: The bill directs federal guidance on covering doula and midwife services under Medicaid and CHIP, streamlines enrollment of out-of-state maternity providers, and expands Commissioned Corps staffing in areas that lost obstetric care — broadening the paid maternal care workforce serving Medicaid patients.

Plans would have been required to pass through the higher minimum hospital payment rates for maternity care, modestly compressing their margins, while their enrollees gained guaranteed postpartum coverage and expanded services.
